extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in democratic institutions, law, and civic institutions
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of jury and democratic stability
extracted.subtask_description: Examination of how legal institutions (lawyers, judges, juries) and geographic/social conditions support or threaten a democratic republic, with emphasis on the United States. Includes normative claims about composition, function, and political effects of the jury and legal profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal profession's conservatism and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws are esteemed not so much because they are good as because they are old; lawyers (especially English) focus on the letter and tradition and would rather use absurd expedients than admit innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains English lawyers' attachment to tradition and letter of the law, contrasted with the role of lawyers in American society; uses metaphors (old tree stock with grafted shoots) and notes that lawyers mix aristocratic tastes with professional interests. Serves as a criterion to evaluate how a legal profession's disposition toward tradition vs. innovation shapes national institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawyers as a counterpoise to democratic excess
rubrics_metrics.description: The lawyers as a body form the most powerful, if not the only, counterpoise to the democratic element in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes how legal counsellors check popular passion by opposing democratic instincts with aristocratic and conservative tendencies (attachment to antiquity, procrastination, narrow views). Use this to assess the balancing role of the bar and bench in restraining sudden democratic impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence (security of tenure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The security of judges' positions (protection against removal or frequent re-election) is crucial; innovations allowing removal or election of judges will have fatal consequences for judicial power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that some State constitutions permit removal at legislature request or election/re-election of judges and predicts these innovations undermine judicial independence. Use as a standard to evaluate constitutional and institutional protections for judges' tenure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge's political power via constitutional review
rubrics_metrics.description: Armed with the power of declaring the laws to be unconstitutional, the magistrate perpetually interferes in political affairs and thereby exercises political influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that while judges cannot make laws, they can prevent the people from acting inconsistently with their own principles by enforcing constitutions; this is a criterion for assessing the political reach of the judiciary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury as a pre-eminent political institution (composition linked to electorate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury is pre-eminently a political institution and must be regarded as one form of the sovereignty of the people; the list of citizens qualified to serve on juries must increase and diminish with the list of electors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that juries are a portion of the nation entrusted with law execution analogous to legislative bodies making law; thus juror qualification should track suffrage. Use to evaluate jury selection rules and whether they reflect popular sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of jury to civil causes increases political influence
rubrics_metrics.description: When the influence of the jury is extended to civil causes its application is constantly palpable and it penetrates into the usages of life, fashioning the human mind and associating itself with the idea of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts limited criminal jury use (occasional action) with civil juries (pervasive impact). Use to assess the broader civic and cultural effects of applying juries to civil litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury as civic education (public school effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury contributes powerfully to form the judgment and to increase the natural intelligence of a people; it may be regarded as a gratuitous public school in which every juror learns to exercise rights and becomes practically acquainted with the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how jury service exposes citizens to legal argument, judge's direction, and the law itself, attributing practical intelligence and political good sense (especially in Americans) to the long use of civil juries. Use as a criterion for measuring civic education delivered by legal institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social composition of juries (aristocratic vs. democratic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The institution of the jury may be aristocratic or democratic depending on the social class from which jurors are selected; in England juries historically come from the aristocracy, while in the United States juries are drawn from the whole people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzes consequences: aristocratic juries reinforce an 'aristocratic republic' while democratic juries reflect and amplify popular sovereignty. Use to evaluate how the social makeup of juries influences the character of governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge's authority amplified through civil juries
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the jury seems to restrict magistracy rights, it actually consolidates judicial power: in civil causes the judge guides jurors, points their attention to the precise question, and puts the answer to the question of law into their mouths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes how judges become trusted authorities whose influence extends beyond courts into legislative assemblies and public life. Use to assess indirect social authority conferred on judges by jury procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury as institutional means to limit and improve judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: By introducing the jury into courts you diminish the number of judges, avoid creating many dependent or half-enlightened magistrates, and preserve judicial independence and quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote argument: many judges lead to vacancies, ambition, dependence on appointing powers, and mediocre tribunals; prefer a skilful judge directing jurors to a majority of imperfect judges. Use as institutional design criterion regarding court size and the balance of judge/jury roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three principal causes maintaining a democratic republic
rubrics_metrics.description: All causes which contribute to the maintenance of the democratic republic in the United States are reducible to three heads: (I) the peculiar and accidental situation in which Providence has placed the Americans; (II) the laws; (III) the manners and customs of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a tripartite framework for analyzing democratic stability: geography/fortune, legal-institutional arrangements, and social mores. Use as a high-level rubric to categorize factors preserving democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic/providential causes favorable to democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidental circumstances—no neighbors, no metropolis, chances of birth in their favor, America an empty country—contribute powerfully to maintaining the democratic republic by reducing wars, taxes, and military needs and by offering boundless land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how geographic isolation reduces threats that create military glory and centralized power, and how abundant land preserves equality and prosperity. Use to evaluate external and material conditions that support democratic institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban concentration as a threat to republican stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of a dominant metropolis helps sustain republican institutions; conversely, large cities with dangerous populations and corrupt local governments constitute a real danger to the democratic republic and may cause its perish unless countervailed by an armed force controlled by the majority but independent of town populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses the influence of city populace (riots, corruption) and the preponderance of capital cities as a serious blow to representative systems; cites 19th-century American urban unrest as an example. Use to evaluate risks posed by metropolitan concentration and social composition of cities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military glory undermines republics
rubrics_metrics.description: Military glory tends to be more formidable to republics than war or taxation; a people carried away by the illusions of glory is dangerous to republican government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the example of General Jackson, elevated by recollection of victory rather than governing competence, to illustrate how military fame can produce poor leadership and threaten democratic stability. Use to assess the political risks of militarism and hero-worship.
